plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a labeled cross-sectional diagram of a Hall-Héroult electrolytic cell used for the industrial production of aluminum metal from Al2O3 dissolved in molten cryolite (Na3AlF6). The outermost structure consists of a steel shell lined with ceramic insulation; inside, two large rectangular carbon anodes (+) are suspended from above into a green-tinted electrolyte layer representing Al2O3 dissolved in molten Na3AlF6, while a sloped carbon cathode (−) forms the entire floor of the cell. White dots surrounding the anodes represent bubbles of O2, CO, and CO2 that form as the carbon anodes are oxidized during electrolysis, and molten aluminum — reduced from Al3+ at the cathode — collects as a dense liquid layer above the cathode floor; a solid crust of electrolyte forms at the top surface of the melt. Gaseous HF and particulates generated during operation are routed upward through an exhaust line labeled "HF and particulates exhaust to filter plant," reflecting the environmental management demands of the process. This figure establishes the Hall-Héroult cell as the primary industrial route for aluminum smelting, highlighting how dissolving Al2O3 in molten Na3AlF6 lowers the operating temperature below what pure Al2O3 would require and how the simultaneous oxidation of the carbon anodes produces mixed gaseous byproducts.

interactionPlan.concept: The Hall-Héroult cell extracts pure aluminum from alumina via electrolysis, reducing aluminum ions into a molten layer at the cathode and oxidizing oxygen at the consumable carbon anodes.
elements: dark gray outer rectangular frame (Steel shell)
light orange/peach inner lining (Ceramic)
black, slightly sloped bottom layer (Carbon cathode (-))
silver/gray metallic liquid layer (Molten aluminum)
thick green liquid layer (Al₂O₃ dissolved in molten Na₃AlF₆)
thin solid top layer across the green liquid (Crust)
two large black rectangular blocks suspended from above (Carbon anodes (+))
positive electrical terminal and horizontal mounting rod
negative electrical terminal and wire connected to the cathode
exhaust hood and upward arrow at top left
white bubble clusters surrounding the submerged portions of the anodes
animated Al³⁺ ions migrating downward toward the cathode
animated O²⁻ ions migrating upward toward the anodes

interactions.label: Play electrolysis
interactions.teaches: Electrolysis is a continuous dynamic process: Al³⁺ ions constantly migrate to the cathode to form a liquid pool, while O²⁻ ions migrate to the anodes to form rising gas bubbles.

interactions.label: Applied current
interactions.teaches: Increasing the current accelerates the redox reactions, leading to a faster accumulation of molten aluminum and a higher rate of gas evolution at the anodes.

demo_steps.title: Cell Components
demo_steps.narration: The cell is heavily insulated with ceramic and lined with carbon. Alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite (the green layer) to lower its melting point, allowing electrolysis at practical temperatures.

demo_steps.title: The Electrolytic Process
demo_steps.narration: When current is applied, Al³⁺ is reduced to dense molten aluminum at the cathode, pooling at the bottom. Simultaneously, O²⁻ is oxidized at the carbon anodes, producing CO and CO₂ gas bubbles.

demo_steps.title: Scaling Production
demo_steps.narration: Ramping up the applied current increases the rate of the redox reactions. The bubble formation becomes more vigorous, and the molten aluminum layer thickens more quickly.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The applied current simultaneously drives two transformations: reducing aluminum ions into a dense liquid layer at the bottom, and oxidizing oxygen to form gases that gradually consume the carbon anodes.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Maintain the distinct horizontal stratification: the black sloped cathode at the bottom, silver molten aluminum in the middle, and green electrolyte on top. The two carbon anodes should be massive and deeply submerged in the green layer, surrounded by white bubble clusters. Ensure the cathode is noticeably sloped to one side to imply how liquid aluminum is eventually tapped off. Include the exhaust duct at the top left and exactly reproduce all labels and leader lines.

authoredContext:
The preparation of aluminum utilizes a process invented in 1886 by Charles M. Hall , who began to work on the problem while a student at Oberlin College in Ohio. Paul L. T. Héroult discovered the process independently a month or two later in France. In honor to the two inventors, this electrolysis cell is known as the Hall–Héroult cell . The Hall–Héroult cell is an electrolysis cell for the production of aluminum. illustrates the Hall–Héroult cell.

The next step is to remove the precipitated aluminum hydroxide by filtration. Heating the hydroxide produces aluminum oxide, Al 2 O 3 , which dissolves in a molten mixture of cryolite, Na 3 AlF 6 , and calcium fluoride, CaF 2 . Electrolysis of this solution takes place in a cell like that shown in . Reduction of aluminum ions to the metal occurs at the cathode, while oxygen, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide form at the anode.

An electrolytic cell is used for the production of aluminum. The electrolysis of a solution of cryolite and calcium fluoride results in aluminum metal at the cathode, and oxygen, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide at the anode.

A diagram is shown. At the center of the diagram are two black squares, each labeled, “Carbon anode ( positive sign ),” and connected by forked tubes to a horizontal tube labeled with a positive sign. The carbon anodes are submerged in a green liquid labeled, “A l subscript 2 O subscript 3 dissolved in molten N a subscript 3 A l F subscript 6.” It is held in place by a three-sided, double layered container which is labeled, “Steel sheet,” on the outer layer and, “Ceramic,” on the inner layer. The carbon anodes are surrounded by bubbles labeled, “Bubbles of O subscript 2, C O, and C O subscript 2.” Below the green liquids lies a silver layer labeled, “Molten aluminum,” and a black layer labeled, “Carbon cathode ( negative sign ).” Above the diagram is an outlet tube labeled with an upward-facing arrow and the words, “H F and particulates exhaust to filter plant.”

discrepancies: The tapping pipe/channel on the right side for extracting the molten aluminum is completely missing.
The upward arrow (↑) indicating flow direction is missing from the exhaust label at the top left.
The crust layer is colored light green, failing to visually distinguish it from the green electrolyte below it (the source uses a tan/brown matching the ceramic).
The left-side labels ('Ceramic' and 'Steel shell') overlap the tank wall geometry in the rendered output, making them hard to read.
The dense, contiguous layer of static white bubbles clinging to the carbon anodes is missing, with only a few scattered background dots present instead.
evaluation.notes: The animated interactive electrolysis simulation is exceptional and pedagogically valuable, but the diagram misses the physical tapping pipe used to extract the aluminum, and left-aligned text placement issues cause labels to overlap the tank structure.
action_items: Add a horizontal tapping pipe or channel passing through the right-side steel and ceramic walls at the height of the molten aluminum layer.
Prepend an upward arrow (↑) to the 'HF and particulates exhaust...' text, or draw a distinct arrow path above the hood.
Change the fill color of the crust rectangle to a tan or brown (e.g., '#c4a484') to match the source and distinguish it from the green electrolyte.

Explicitly apply `.attr({ 'text-anchor': 'end' })` to the 'Ceramic' and 'Steel shell' labels (or use a smaller `x` value with default left-alignment) to prevent them from rendering on top of the left tank wall.
